brave.title: US v. Chafin, No. 25-4521 (4th Cir. 2026) :: Justia
brave.snippet:
The defendant, after pleading guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm, received a below-Guidelines prison sentence followed by supervised release. Upon commencing supervision, he repeatedly violated its conditions, including using illegal drugs, failing to report for drug testing, skipping required addiction recovery meetings, and not paying a special assessment.
The court rejected this argument, relying on circuit precedent from United States v. Lewis, and imposed the revocation sentence. The defendant then appealed, arguing that the Supreme Court’s subsequent decision in Esteras v. United States abrogated the Fourth Circuit’s approach in Lewis.
The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reviewed the case. The court reaffirmed that its prior decision in Lewis remains valid, holding that a district court may lawfully impose a revocation sentence to sanction a defendant’s breach of the court’s trust.
The Fourth Circuit explained that Esteras did not abrogate Lewis, as Esteras only barred consideration of retribution for the original offense, not the need to sanction a breach of supervised release conditions. The court concluded that the district court had not procedurally erred and that the revocation sentence was reasonable. Accordingly, the Fourth Circuit affirmed the judgment of the district court.

No. 17–1657. Argued February 20, 2019—Decided May 20, 2019 Petitioner Mission Product Holdings, Inc., entered into a contract with Respondent Tempnology, LLC, which gave Mission a license to use Tempnology’s trademarks in connection with the distribution of certain clothing and accessories. Tempnology filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and sought to reject its agreement with Mission. Section 365 of the Bankruptcy Code enables a debtor to “reject any executory contract”—meaning a contract that neither party has finished performing. 11 U. S. C. §365(a) . It further provides that rejection “constitutes a breach of such contract.” §365(g).

   But the Court of Appeals for the First Circuit rejected the Panel’s and Seventh Circuit’s view, and reinstated the Bankruptcy Court decision terminating Mission’s license. See  In re Tempnology, LLC , 879 F. 3d 389 (2018). The majority first endorsed that court’s inference from Section 365(n) and similar provisions. It next reasoned that special features of trademark law counsel against allowing a licensee to retain rights to a mark after the licensing agreement’s rejection. Under that body of law, the major- ity stated, the trademark owner’s “[f]ailure to monitor and exercise [quality] control” over goods associated with a trademark “jeopardiz[es] the continued validity of [its] own trademark rights.”  Id., at 402. So if (the majority continued) a licensee can keep using a mark after an agreement’s rejection, the licensor will need to carry on its monitoring activities. And according to the majority, that would frustrate “Congress’s principal aim in providing for rejection”: to “release the debtor’s estate from burdensome obligations.”  Ibid.  (internal quotation marks omitted).  Judge Torruella dissented, mainly for the Seventh Circuit’s reasons. See  id., at 405–407.

RUSHING, Circuit Judge:
Andrew Chafin violated the conditions of his supervised release and received a nine-
month prison sentence.  He appeals, arguing that the district court impermissibly
considered the need to sanction his breach of trust when determining his revocation
sentence.  In United States v. Lewis, our Court rejected this argument and held that a district
court may lawfully impose a revocation sentence to sanction a defendant’s breach of its
trust.  90 F.4th 288, 299 (4th Cir.), cert. denied, 144 S. Ct. 2543 (2024).  Chafin contends
that the Supreme Court’s subsequent decision in Esteras v. United States, 145 S. Ct. 2031
(2025), abrogated this Court’s holding.  We conclude that Lewis is still good law; therefore,
we affirm.

octen.title: Fourth Circuit affirms nine-month prison sentence for Chafin | LAWS.com News
octen.snippet:
The Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals has upheld a nine-month prison sentence for Andrew Chafin, who violated the terms of his supervised release. This ruling affects Chafin, who had previously been convicted of possessing a firearm as a felon, and it underscores the court's stance on handling breaches of supervised release conditions.
Chafin's case began after he pleaded guilty to a felony firearm charge under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1). Following his conviction, he was sentenced to a term of imprisonment and was later placed on supervised release in May 2025. However, Chafin struggled to comply with the conditions of his release, leading to multiple violations including drug use and failure to report to his probation officer. In August 2025, his probation officer filed a petition to revoke his supervised release.
During the revocation hearing, Chafin admitted to the violations and expressed a desire to return to supervision. The government, however, argued for a significant prison sentence to encourage Chafin to reform. The district court ultimately decided to revoke Chafin's supervised release, citing the need to deter future violations and to address Chafin's ongoing substance abuse issues.
The court's ruling was based on several factors outlined in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a), including the nature of Chafin's violations and the need for deterrence. The district court stated, "We are hoping maybe this will slam some sense into him," indicating a belief that a prison sentence could help Chafin recognize the seriousness of his actions.

parallel.title: United States v. Chafin — Fourth Circuit upheld a revocation sentence based partly on breach of trust – Case Law Wire
parallel.snippet:
On appeal, Chafin argued that considering breach of trust made his sentence procedurally unreasonable. Although he acknowledged that United States v. Lewis permitted that consideration, he contended that the Supreme Court’s subsequent decision in Esteras v. United States had abrogated Lewis.

The Court’s Holding

The Fourth Circuit affirmed, holding that Lewis remains binding after Esteras. Esteras prohibits a revocation court from considering retribution for the defendant’s original crime of conviction, but it expressly left unresolved whether a court may sanction a defendant’s breach of trust arising from violations of supervised-release conditions—the issue Lewis had decided.
The court rejected Chafin’s argument that breach of trust is an unlisted sentencing factor. Section 3583(e) incorporates the applicable Sentencing Guidelines and policy statements, including Chapter Seven’s direction that revocation sentences primarily sanction the defendant’s breach of trust. Considering the seriousness of that breach can also inform permissible, forward-looking goals such as deterrence, protection of the public, and rehabilitation.
Because the district court did not punish Chafin again for his original firearm offense or punish him for new criminal conduct, its reliance on his repeated supervision violations and breach of trust was lawful. Its explanation showed that the nine-month sentence served permissible statutory purposes and was procedurally reasonable.

Key Takeaways

* Esteras did not abrogate Fourth Circuit precedent permitting revocation sentences to sanction a defendant’s breach of the court’s trust.
* A revocation court may not impose punishment based on retribution for the original crime of conviction.
* Chapter Seven’s breach-of-trust framework is a permissible consideration because Section 3583(e) expressly incorporates relevant Guidelines and policy statements.

seltz.snippet:
The First Amendment protects both book buyers and booksellers. Does the Second Amendment protect only people who buy guns, or does it also protect people who sell guns? Though this question has divided the federal courts, the answer is quite clear: operating a business that provides Second Amendment services is protected by the Second Amendment. *District of Columbia v. Heller*1 teaches that regulation of how firearms are commercially sold enjoys a presumption of constitutionality, which does not extend to prohibitions of firearms sales.

In the lower federal courts, there is a developing split about whether firearms sellers have Second Amendment rights which the courts are bound to respect. Seventh Circuit courts view firearms sellers like booksellers — as holders of constitutional rights. While gun sellers are subject to much stricter regulation than are booksellers, they are both protected by the Bill of Rights. Conversely, in the courts of the Fourth Circuit, gun sellers have no Second Amendment rights.

*Brown v. Board of Education*2 was not exactly a popular decision among some state and local governments, and among some lower court judges. The same is true of *Heller*. One form of resistance to *Heller* has been to read the opinion in the narrowest possible way, excluding from Second Amendment protection many normal activities involving firearms. One such form of resistance is the claim that the Second Amendment does not apply to gun sales.

By this theory, because the Second Amendment is an individual right to have arms for self-defense, the Second Amendment does not apply to corporations that provide services to gun owners, such as selling them guns. Likewise, since the Second Amendment is a right to have a gun for self-defense, the Second Amendment has nothing to do with anyone who sells or gives away a firearm.

Esteras , 145 S. Ct. at 2042 .  ... Chafin concedes that the district court did not rely on any purported need to sanction him for his original offense of conviction. And the court did not impose the revocation sentence “as punishment for new criminal conduct.” Id. at 296. Instead, the court identified the permissible Section 3553 (a) factors, addressed Chafin’s numerous violations of his supervised release conditions, and explained why a revocation sentence was necessary to deter Chafin and assist his rehabilitation.

The defendant, after pleading guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm, received a below-Guidelines prison sentence followed by supervised release. Upon commencing supervision, he repeatedly violated its conditions, including using illegal drugs, failing to report for drug testing, skipping required addiction recovery meetings, and not paying a special assessment.
The court rejected this argument, relying on circuit precedent from United States v. Lewis, and imposed the revocation sentence. The defendant then appealed, arguing that the Supreme Court’s subsequent decision in Esteras v. United States abrogated the Fourth Circuit’s approach in Lewis.
The United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reviewed the case. The court reaffirmed that its prior decision in Lewis remains valid, holding that a district court may lawfully impose a revocation sentence to sanction a defendant’s breach of the court’s trust.
The Fourth Circuit explained that Esteras did not abrogate Lewis, as Esteras only barred consideration of retribution for the original offense, not the need to sanction a breach of supervised release conditions. The court concluded that the district court had not procedurally erred and that the revocation sentence was reasonable. Accordingly, the Fourth Circuit affirmed the judgment of the district court.
